bull_bear.body: - FY27 capex ₹1,500cr (frontloaded). Conservative guidance, broad-based capacity ahead of demand.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- Metal-price / war / freight volatility → near-term demand & margin (the headline risk this call).
- Middle-East exposure: oil sourcing (Saudi Aramco Yanbu refinery — still running) + sales to Saudi/Kuwait/Iraq subdued until war ends.
- New competition: **UltraTech (Aditya Birla) + Adani** entering wires/cables (mostly building wires/LDC — mgmt says limited threat to specialty); a new conductor entrant with "carbon-core" tech near PGCIL approval (past-performance tender requirement is a barrier).
- US Section 232: 50% on conductors (Al), 25% on cables — now stable (certainty = positive); US imports ~90% Al (so US producers also pay duty) vs <5% Cu → Al exports less disadvantaged.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: - Conservative guidance (under-promises margins), candid on near-term headwinds, deeply entrenched (sole HVDC-oil supplier; CTC pressure from transformer OEMs). Frontloading capex on conviction in the multi-year cycle.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **Two-speed read:** structural demand intact, but Apar is the one name flagging a *real near-term air-pocket* (metal prices + war) — a useful caution vs the suppliers riding the shortage. Watch whether others echo this next quarter.
- **Apar confirms KSH's thesis from the buyer side:** CTC was in "major domestic deficit" — Apar (a CTC maker itself) prioritized domestic transformer OEMs and only now exports.
- **HVDC transformer-oil monopoly** (Hitachi/GE/Siemens) is a quiet, high-moat annuity as HVDC awards flow FY27–28.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Balance sheet remains conservatively geared with a debt/equity ratio of 0.16x in FY26 versus 0.10x in FY24 and FY25, despite the step-up in capex.
- Growth is being funded largely from internal accruals, with capex rising to Rs 736.66 crore in FY26 while working capital was Rs 3,252.86 crore.
- Capex is spread across segments rather than concentrated — conductors, oils and cables all received investment across FY24-FY26.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Global scale leadership: world's largest manufacturer of aluminium and alloy conductors and largest exporter of conductors from India; world's third-largest and India's largest transformer oil manufacturer; among the top five CTC/PICC makers globally.
- Raw-material cost advantage: two Odisha conductor plants sit next to aluminium smelters, allowing use of liquid molten aluminium directly rather than buying and re-melting ingots as the industry does.
- Logistics advantage: four conductor plants in Dadra & Nagar Haveli near Mumbai ports and cable plants ~150 km from the Mumbai sea port; all export plants located near seaports and international airports.
- Product innovation and R&D depth: in-house R&D with NABL-accredited labs across plants and 2000+ testing scope; pioneer of AL-59, HTLS reconductoring turnkey solutions, live-line OPGW installation, harness solutions, MVCC (first Indian manufacturer) and E-beam HR FR EBXL wires (first in India).
- Certification and approval moat in export markets: highest number of UL compliance certificates in India and 19 UL approvals for US cable supply -- a barrier new entrants find difficult to replicate.
- Distribution and diversification: presence in 140+ countries with 4000+ global clients, a 350+ product range and customers spread across utilities, developers, EPCs and multiple geographies, limiting concentration risk.
- Approved-vendor positions that are hard to displace: India's largest maker of copper conductors for railway electrification and the only approved Indian vendor supplying copper conductors to the Ahmedabad-Mumbai bullet train project; major supplier of speciality elastomeric cables to Indian Navy establishments and DRDO.
- Technology and brand tie-ups: ACCC conductor technology tie-up with CTC Global (USA) and an auto-lubricant licensing agreement with ENI, Italy for the ENI brand.
- Manufacturing breadth: eleven operating plants in India and overseas, India's largest E-beam plant installation and five E-beam irradiation facilities in the cable business.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Geopolitical disruption and tariffs — US tariff actions and shipping-route disruption affecting exports and commodity prices — Management's first-listed principal risk: geopolitical events may put pressure on commodity prices and export dynamics, and the FY26 MD&A notes the outbreak of war in the Middle East plus a sudden US tariff hike that subdued part-year performance. Mitigants cited are a footprint in more than 140 countries, domestic infrastructure/renewables capex demand, and full hedging of metal prices so metal-price moves are limited and passed through to customers.
- Export concentration exposed to de-globalisation and local-manufacturing policies — Exports contribute roughly 30% of turnover (29.77% of the entity's total turnover per BRSR), so localisation initiatives by importing countries directly threaten growth. The Company's response is to evaluate alternative manufacturing locations on raw-material availability and cost economics, and it already runs an oils plant in the UAE and has incorporated overseas subsidiaries in the USA, Saudi Arabia and Brazil.
- Intensifying competition — new entrants on premium products and Chinese competition in overseas markets — New players may use aggressive pricing that affects operating margin, and Chinese competition has been intensifying in overseas exports, especially from countries with trade surpluses that enjoy an advantage over India in some markets. APAR's defence is product differentiation (AL-59, harness solutions, covered conductors, reconductoring services, special-grade oils, Fire Protekt house wires), unique alloying capability, and market-leadership positions with long-standing customer relationships.
- Capex payback risk on long-term expansion projects — Directly flagged: payback on long-term capex may be hurt by timely material availability, market growth, demand conditions and achievement of planned capacity utilisation. This risk is amplified by the front-loaded FY27 capex plan and compressed rollout schedules; mitigation is phased capacity addition across divisions, ordering machinery well ahead of long delivery timelines, and building contingencies into the payback working.
- Customer and geography concentration — dependence on utilities, EPC contractors and infrastructure players in a limited set of regions — The Company states that overexposure to specific markets or customer categories may increase earnings volatility and limit its ability to absorb external shocks. Diversification across utilities, developers and EPCs and across North America, South America, the Middle East and Europe is the stated mitigant; separately, no single customer contributes more than ten percent of Group revenue.
- Commodity, forex, interest-rate and customer-credit risk in a working-capital-heavy business — Aluminium and copper price, forex and interest-rate exposure are managed through well-established hedging principles, prompt hedging on a pricing formula, natural hedges and forward covers, with metal gain/loss and forex plus working-capital interest built into customer pricing as a full pass-through. Credit risk is managed with structured customer evaluation, credit limits, credit-securing processes and in-house business-legal teams; DSO stood at 85 days against 82 days a year earlier, on a debt-equity ratio of 0.16 versus 0.10.
- Climate, extreme-weather and energy-cost risk to a geographically clustered manufacturing base — Two conductor plants are in cyclone-exposed Odisha (Jharsuguda and Sambalpur) and the cable plants in Gujarat plus five conductor plants in nearby Dadra & Nagar Haveli sit in a single western cluster, with four to five cyclonic storms forming near India each year. Higher energy costs are separately flagged as a material risk from rising production, grid tariffs and fossil-fuel rates. Mitigations include design strengthening, covered sheds, flood-management systems with water-collection pits and heavy-capacity evacuation pumps, business continuity and disaster-recovery plans, TCFD scenario analysis, energy audits at all plants, and raising renewable energy to 10.9% of the electricity mix in FY26 from 3.7% in FY23.
- Cybersecurity threats to operations and sensitive data — Unauthorised access or inadvertent disclosure could cause reputational damage, financial and operational losses and legal liabilities. The response is a CIA-triad strategy on a Zero Trust Network Architecture, periodic third-party VAPT, phishing-simulation and awareness training, enterprise-grade firewalls, IDS/IPS and antivirus/EDR, with ISO 27001 implementation in progress.
- Talent availability, retention and succession — Inability to attract, nurture and retain talent, and absence of succession planning, could affect operational continuity — material for a technology-differentiated manufacturer where attrition also risks loss of critical technical expertise. Mitigation includes developing N-1 successors, Great Place to Work surveys, annual industry-level compensation benchmarking, the newly introduced ESAR scheme for select senior employees, and knowledge-management systems.
- Carbon border taxes and the need to sustain growth in new sectors and geographies — The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism is flagged as a potential financial impact, though management assesses it as minimal because most customers are in the US, Canada and Latin America, while it works to cut carbon intensity and raise the share of low-carbon raw material and scrap. Separately, management flags that new sectors, segments or geographies must continually be identified to sustain the growth momentum.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- Clean energy: **50GW+ added FY26** (highest ever); non-fossil 250–270GW; solar 140GW+ (record +54GW FY26); wind +6GW.
- **Transformation capacity +113,000 MVA FY26** (+30% YoY, ~11% below the 126k target); **48% at 765kV**.
- Data centres: 1.5–1.7GW → **5GW by 2030** (7–8GW optimistic), >$30bn investment.
- NEP to 2032: transmission 5L→6.5L ckm; transformation 1,429→2,354 GVA; interregional 120→143GW (2027)→168GW (2032).
business.title: Macro backdrop (useful sector data)

business.body:
- **Short-term slowdown in ordering** — aluminium price + premiums (MJP) up, freight/war premiums at all-time highs, Middle-East containers shipping without full insurance → **projects deferred/delayed**; customers postpone deliveries (even OPGW/fibre, costs up 3–4x).
- **Manpower/port issues** from elections (Bihar/West Bengal/NE) slowing project execution.
- Domestic capacity additions → some pricing pressure; Chinese competition; LME–SHFE aluminium gap $330–360/t.
- *But:* "structurally, energy-infrastructure fundamentals remain intact" — expects a 2H-weighted year (like FY26).

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers (listed names)

business.body:
- Claims #1 position in India by conductor sales in FY26 and is one of the leading global aluminium and alloy conductor manufacturers as of March 2026, alongside being one of India's leading exporters of conductors and cables.
- India's largest private sector manufacturer of specialty oils by installed capacity as of March 2026, and one of the largest cable manufacturers for the domestic renewables segment.
- 68-year legacy operating 11 facilities globally with corporate presence in six countries (India, UAE, Saudi Arabia, USA, Singapore, Brazil) and ~2,200 employees.
- Serves a diversified global customer base across T&D, mobility, telecom, infrastructure, renewables, data centres and defence, positioned around three themes: Carrying Electricity, Client-First Innovation and Engineered Performance.
- Growth is framed around established drivers (renewables, transmission, infrastructure, public transport, telecom, China+1) plus two newer drivers witnessed in the last two years — data centre buildout and energy storage systems.

business.body:

- [Receivables quality] 50.40% of FY26 receivables are secured under various means and a further 25.40% are from government transmission and sector-specific companies, leaving 24.20% as others.
- [Export franchise] Export mix was 29.77% in FY26, having moderated from 32.82% in FY24, with exports of Rs 6,817.96 crore in FY26.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: APAR manufactures conductors, power and telecom cables, speciality oils and lubricants, and polymers, largely for the power transmission and distribution value chain. Customers include utilities and transmission/distribution companies, EPC and transmission contractors, renewable developers, OEMs, Indian Railways, defence establishments, data centres and industrial/pharma/cosmetics buyers of speciality oils, alongside distributors and channel partners. Roughly three-tenths of turnover comes from exports across Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia and the Americas, with the balance from a domestic market driven by grid expansion and renewables integration.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Product premiumisation across all three segments -- shifting the mix towards higher-value offerings such as HTLS and AL59 conductors, CTC for transformers, and specialised cables (aerospace, fire-survival, solar, wind, defence, naval) where performance, safety and reliability command better economics.
- Front-loading strategic capacity: compressing multi-year rollout schedules, including fast-tracking a three-year cable programme, so that manufacturing capacity is online ahead of the demand curve in an industry where commissioning timelines are lengthening.
- Explicitly sizing cable capacity for wind, solar and data-centre infrastructure rather than treating renewable energy as an incidental driver, alongside aggressive de-bottlenecking in the conductor and lubricants divisions.
- Global expansion and localisation: building sales, distribution and contractor/asset-aggregator approvals in the USA -- the world's largest cable market -- while pursuing CTC exports with initial approvals in the Middle East and work toward US and European certifications.
- Securing stringent technical certifications as a competitive barrier -- the highest number of UL-certified products among Indian cable manufacturers.
- Moving beyond traditional products into technology-led adjacencies: Telecom Solutions expanding into high-capacity fibre, submarine and drone-based connectivity and the Kavach project for Indian Railways; oils expanding with substation growth.
- Expanding presence in higher-value, application-specific segments created by industrial automation, Industry 4.0 and IoT, while simultaneously adopting automation and Industry 4.0 in APAR's own manufacturing to deepen cost competitiveness.
- Positioning the conductor business as a strategic partner in grid modernisation rather than a component supplier, built on two pillars: domestic strengthening with value migration to higher value-added offerings, and global market breakthroughs, particularly in the US after the rationalisation of US tariff rates.
- Prioritising forward-looking capital allocation over short-term reporting cycles to maximise long-term shareholder value and secure market leadership for the decade ahead.
- Anchoring ESG and customer-centricity in the growth strategy, including low-carbon products and community programmes across healthcare, education, rural development and gender equality.
- Complete hedging policy on commodities so that metal price movements do not affect profitability.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: APAR executed `740 crore of capital expenditure in FY26 and has guided to an accelerated FY27 capex of `1,500 crore, describing this as proactively front-loading capital allocation. Management says that in an industry where commissioning timelines are lengthening it has compressed its multi-year rollout schedules -- including fast-tracking a three-year cable programme -- so that manufacturing capacity is online ahead of the demand curve. The investment spans all three business segments: cable capacity is being explicitly sized to capture Wind, Solar and Data Centre infrastructure demand rather than treating renewables as an incidental driver, and this is paired with aggressive de-bottlenecking in the conductor and lubricants divisions. Management frames these targeted expansions as solidifying a multi-year growth runway across T&D grids, global export corridors and hyperscale data centres. The physical footprint at year end comprises eleven manufacturing plants -- ten in India and one in Sharjah, UAE -- namely conductors at Athola Unit-3, Athola Unit-5, Khanvel and Rakholi (Silvassa, Dadra and Nagar Haveli) and at Jharsuguda and Lapanga in Odisha, a co-located oil plant in Silvassa, oils and lubricants at Rabale (Navi Mumbai), cables and telecom at Khatalwada and polymers at Umbergaon in Gujarat, plus oils and lubricants (PSF) at Sharjah -- supported by 26 depots in India and 2 overseas and 12 offices in India and overseas. Alongside manufacturing capacity, APAR is investing in digital and energy infrastructure: smart-factory ecosystems with real-time oversight of production, quality and energy use, advanced analytics for demand forecasting and input control, and Industry 4.0 / IoT adoption across operations, with management stating it has 'locked in bold horizons with targets for the next 24-36 months' tied to sustainability pledges including net-zero emissions and circular-economy loops. On the energy side, three wind-solar hybrid plants were commissioned in June 2023, October 2025 and March 2026 in partnership with a leading supplier, and rooftop solar has been deployed at all major plants, lifting renewable energy to 10.9% of the electricity mix in FY 2025-26 from 3.7% in FY 2022-23. The named-disclosure blocks for capital commitments and segment capital expenditure supplied with this bundle carried headings only and no figures, so no rupee capex quantum is recorded below.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- A multi-decadal electrification cycle: global electricity demand is expected to rise at an average annual rate of 3.6% over the 2026-2030 forecast period, with a structural shift toward energy security and diversified power generation.
- Domestic T&D pipeline: management says APAR is capturing high-value shares of a `9 Tn (US$96.7 billion) domestic T&D pipeline through 2032, with the National Electricity Plan 2023-32 targeting 6.48 lakh ckm of transmission network and 2,345 GVA of transformation capacity by 2032.
- AI compute and hyperscale data centres described as a new structural growth driver, not a peripheral opportunity -- every additional unit of AI compute requires proportionately more high-quality power delivery, MV/LV cabling, busbars, transformers and conductors engineered for higher load densities; the global data-centre cable market is projected to grow from US$12.24 bn in 2026 to US$18.81 bn by 2032 and hyperscalers are expected to spend ~US$600 bn of capex in 2026.
- Renewables build-out: global renewable capacity expanded by a record 692 GW in 2025 and India added ~51 GW in FY2025-26 including a record 44.61 GW of solar and 6.05 GW of wind, driving demand for specialised cabling and grid infrastructure.
- Grid modernisation and replacement of ageing legacy infrastructure worldwide, shifting the market toward high-efficiency, low-loss conductor technologies (HTLS, HVDC, 765 kV).
- North American demand propelled by grid modernisation and data-centre/industrial electrification -- APAR has already started supplying cables to U.S. data-centre projects and US revenue grew nearly 50% YoY in FY26 despite tariff issues; management expects to build on this momentum.
- European investment driven by decarbonisation mandates, transmission expansion and last-mile upgrades; the newly concluded EU-India FTA eliminating tariffs on over 90% of Indian goods could open incremental opportunity.
- Mix improvement as a margin lever: premium conductors (HTLS and AL59) reached 45.8% of conductor segment revenue in FY26, and the cable business continues moving up the value chain into specialised applications, which management says enhances the resilience of margins.
- Substation-linked oils demand: as power demand grows there is a linear expansion of substations, with POWEROIL transformer oil demand growing at over 10% per annum and copper CTC used in transformer windings up 250% in FY26; these two products comprise 30% of the cost of a transformer.
- Domestic macro support: India remained the fastest-growing major economy with FY26 growth of 7.6%, IMF forecasting 6.5% and the RBI 6.9% for the current year, alongside record Indian Railways capex of `2,93,030 crore in the Union Budget 2026-27, a DoT outlay of `73,990 crore, defence exports up over 60% in 2025-26, and data-centre tax holidays to 2047.
- Headwinds flagged: geopolitical disruption from the Middle East war, rising commodity prices (fully hedged, so not affecting profitability), the US tariff hike under Section 232 (universal by origin, so not competitively disadvantageous, but it subdued part-year performance), and postponement of part of the order book as customers avoided piling up inventory.
- Transformer oil is expected to grow in tandem with the T&D space, though management flags a possible transient phase of slow growth if infrastructure capex spending is delayed or reduced.
- Premium conductors, including HTLS and AL59, account for a little over 50% of the conductor order book (and 45.8% of segment revenue).
- Part of the conductor order book delivery has been postponed as customers preferred not to pile up inventory following the sudden US tariff increase.
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: The diversified T&D bellwether (₹22,902cr, ~29% 5-yr CAGR). Conductors crossed ₹10,000cr at record unit margins; cables now #2 segment (data-centre led); **sole HVDC transformer-oil supplier** to Hitachi/GE/Siemens. Confirms the structural super-cycle *and* that **CTC was in domestic deficit** (now exporting). But uniquely flags a **near-term demand slowdown** — metal-price spikes, war/freight premiums, and election-driven manpower issues are making customers postpone deliveries. Margins guided conservatively to ₹35–36k/MT **+ tailwinds**.

open.item: Copper business (conductors, CTC, busbars) expected to exceed INR3,000 crores next year (FY26).
INR1,300cr capex to be funded ~50:50 by internal accruals/equity (INR650cr) and long-term debt (INR650cr).
After 5 phases of CTC capacity expansion, APAR has begun exporting CTC (Middle East approvals secured) and is pursuing Europe and US approvals to broaden CTC exports in FY27/FY28.

Bushing shortage delaying transformer/substation deliveries and hence transmission-line/CTC/transformer-oil demand; government import concession kicking in within ~1 week and domestic bushing capacity expected in ~6 months.

Near-term demand slowdown flagged: sharp metal (Al/Cu) and freight/war-premium cost increases and specialty-polymer shortages will hit near-term cable/conductor/oil volumes and margins as customers defer deliveries.
US sales expected to grow significantly in FY27 over FY26 (and further in FY28) for both cables and conductors, aided by settled Section 232 tariffs (25% on cables, 50% aluminium conductors).
Conductor volume growth guidance maintained at ~10% year-on-year (FY26 delivered 8.6%).
FY27 capex increased to ~INR1,500 crores (conductor ~INR400cr, oil ~INR200cr, cable ~INR850cr), on top of FY26 capex of INR740 crores, front-loaded for future demand.
APAR is the sole HVDC transformer-oil supplier to Hitachi Energy, GE and Siemens; large HVDC projects just awarded, with oil/conductor order awards to flow through FY27 and FY28.
Cable division targeting ~25% CAGR toward INR10,000 crores (FY26 at INR6,220cr, +25.8%); capex being pulled forward, tracking on/slightly ahead.
Long-term (3-5 year) sustainable conductor EBITDA per metric ton guided at INR28,500 plus tailwinds.

Middle East war severely disrupted oil supply chain (refinery raw-material stranding, April contract supplies down 50%, freight spikes); oil/Specialty exports and some conductor (Iraq) deliveries subdued until the war resolves; supply largely restored in May at higher prices.
Conductor medium-to-long-term EBITDA/ton guidance upgraded to INR35,000-36,000 plus tailwinds (from INR30,000), on premium/reconductoring/copper mix.
US manufacturing set-up still under study given a fluid tariff/policy situation; decision to be taken as clarity emerges.

India-EU FTA expected to be favourable for cable/conductor exports (EU ~5% of revenue; prior tariffs 4-7.5% plus OFC antidumping); pursuing more EU utility approvals, impact to be quantified in a couple of months.
Chinese subsidy (~8-12% on metal) making non-US export markets (Africa, LatAm, Europe, Australia) unattractive; APAR will divert capacity to India rather than compete at a loss; seen as cyclical.
Appointed advisors to explore setting up manufacturing in the US (over and above the announced India/UAE capex) to serve US-made-product utilities and short-delivery demand.
Amended articles of association to permit entry into the energy storage business as a future line; at a very early exploratory stage.
Chinese competition (often below-cost pricing) has intensified and is expected to continue in all markets except India and the US; management will not cut prices merely for volume.
Conductor EBITDA per ton guidance retained at INR28,500 (currently realizing ~INR37,000-38,000 on premium mix).
